title.narrative: Restoring and protecting Biodiversity, Coastal Landscapes, and Climate Change Resilience through Nature Based Solutions, Women and Youth Entrepreneurship in Vanuatu

description.narrative: E.1 Knowledge management and CommunicationThe project will initiate a knowledge gap and learning potential analysis during its first two quarters, overseen by the designated M&E specialist. However, all team members will be responsible for incorporating knowledge management into their roles. During the PPG phase, several key needs for knowledge management have been identified:? The collection and organization of existing knowledge regarding biophysical, productive, and socioeconomic conditions in the four target areas and their associated ecosystems.? The organization, analysis, and interpretation of knowledge generated through the piloting of innovative NbS.? The development of an effective outreach strategy to ensure that NbS pilot results inform policy decisions and attract private and public investments? The dissemination of knowledge generated through NbS pilots to stakeholders, facilitating investment in the four target areas of Vanuatu and potential expansion across the region.? The monitoring of trends in conditions and the effectiveness of NbS in the four target areas and their ecosystems, guiding adaptive policy and investment formulation and implementation.? The sharing of knowledge on challenges, strategies, and results related to the management of the four target areas in Vanuatu and their associated ecosystems across the BGI IP portfolio.The gap analysis will involve interviews with representatives from key government agencies and village-level stakeholders in the four target areas. Additionally, it will entail a review of prevailing reporting templates used by provincial officers (tourism, agriculture, and area administrators) to facilitate ongoing monitoring processes.Building on the results of the knowledge gap analysis, a learning strategy will be developed. This strategy will include the creation of a common reporting template to enhance monitoring, documentation, and sharing of best practices and lessons learned, including failures, at local, regional, and global levels. The reporting template will define indicators and processes for monitoring and evaluating knowledge management and learning objectives.The project’s learning strategy will be integrated with the BGI IP’s community of practice to facilitate effective knowledge exchange and learning among child projects. This will involve regular interaction via the IP’s thematic hubs.In line with FAO’s Knowledge Strategy (2011) and GEF’s knowledge management Approach (2015), the project’s knowledge management strategies include:1) Collaborative and participatory formulation of protocols for monitoring (including environmental quality indicators) and the processing, management and exchange of data;2) The full engagement of institutional and local stakeholders in the formulation and management of NBS pilots, in order to maximize their receptiveness to information on their results; and in the definition of indicators and design of corresponding monitoring protocols, in order to foment their adoption, application and sustained application;3) Targeted capacity enhancement of key stakeholders (based on capacity needs assessment at project start), in order to raise their receptiveness and ability to receive, manage, digest and apply knowledge;4) Engagement of national and regional academic and research institutions, in the collation and generation of knowledge, in its dissemination (through educational curricula and training events), and as repositories of knowledge generated through the project;5) Regular knowledge outreach, through printed and on-line publications and periodic stocktaking and dissemination meetings. E.2 Socio-economic Benefits and Decent Rural Employment[1]The project will support women and youth in Vanuatu currently largely involved in subsistence production to design and develop their own businesses that will be based on NbS they will also co-design. Hence, the project is intended to bring about positive changes for local livelihoods. The project will ensure that its activities do not perpetuate poverty and inequality in socially unsustainable food systems and tourism. While identified health and safety risks are considered as minor, the project will ensure that adequate measures are taken to ensure safety of workers and farmers during these activities aligned with FAO social and environment guidelines.Finally, through the project life-cycle, the project will apply principles, practices and techniques that are best suited to avoiding the violation of, and promoting the application of core international labour standards, other international labour standards relevant to the agri-food sectors, tourism, and national employment and labour laws. [1] Specific guidance on how FAO can promote the Four Pillars of Decent Work in rural areas is provided in the Quick reference for addressing decent rural employment (as well as in the full corresponding Guidance document). For more information on FAO’s work on decent rural employment and related guidance materials please consult the FAO thematic website at: http://www.fao.org/rural-employment/en/.
